threads.title: US-Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz
threads.current_state: Trump says he's nearing a decision framed as whether to 'annihilate' Iran's regime, and claims direct Tehran contact that Iranian officials deny exists. He'll meet Gulf Cooperation Council leaders in New York around September 22; Iran's FM made a second Beijing trip this week. Saudi Aramco is restoring damaged pipeline capacity, easing Brent toward the low $100s even as rhetoric hits new highs. Actual diplomacy remains stalled -- no new Salalah date has been set.

timeline.summary: First tracked: nine nights of US strikes, oil up about 20% this month, 10-day ceasefire being mediated.
10-day ceasefire formally proposed; US strikes continue, Iran calls it full-scale war, Brent tops $91, war cost estimated at $37.5B.
By Wednesday, strikes reach an eleventh consecutive night; Brent pushes past $92, reviving inflation concern.

Ceasefire proposal remains unadopted; Brent closes at $94.13, a five-week high; Strait transits fall to 25 ships from a peak of 49; Saudi coalition vows a forceful response to the Houthi blockade threat.
13th consecutive night of strikes; Iran hits Kuwait and the Houthis strike two Saudi tankers; Brent crosses $100 for the first time since May; Trump considers a massive attack.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard launches a fresh drone attack on Kuwait; sirens sound across Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar; Iran rejects an Iraqi-mediated ceasefire proposal; Brent holds near $100.

US carries out no new strikes overnight for the first time since the ceasefire collapsed; an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran to discuss Strait of Hormuz shipping; Brent eases to about $96.80, down nearly 4% but still up over 12% on the week.

Iran-aligned Houthi rebels fire dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, starting large fires; read as retaliation for Saudi strikes on a Houthi-held Yemeni coastal city.

The pause holds through the weekend into Monday with no new strikes reported on either front; Brent tumbles toward the mid-$80s, down roughly 7% on the session, as Trump signals openness to renewed talks with Tehran.

Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House for the first time since the war began, calling the talks 'positive and productive' and reaffirming a shared commitment against an Iranian nuclear weapon; Brent eases further into the mid-to-high $80s.

Iran says it struck US bases in Jordan and other Gulf locations overnight; Trump vows to hit back hard and repeats a bridge-bombing threat; the US and Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed groups in Iraq; Brent jumps back above $90.

The US launches a 'heavy wave' of new strikes on Iran; Iranian state media reports at least three civilians killed. Iran retaliates against Jordan and Kuwait, killing a worker at a Chinese-owned building in Kuwait. Trump says it is now 'our turn' to hit Iran hard.
Qatar formally condemns Iran's strikes on Jordan and Kuwait as violations of sovereignty - the first significant regional diplomatic reaction against Tehran this round.

Iran's army claims strikes on US assets at Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base; neither government confirms it. The US conducts no fresh strikes overnight - the first pause since Wednesday's heavy wave.

Egypt reports a drone of unknown origin hit two gas vessels at its Damietta port, a possible first sign the conflict is pulling in a new country; Brent eases 1.4% to $87.78 as Hormuz tanker traffic shows tentative recovery.

Kuwait's army confirms it intercepted a fresh wave of Iranian drones aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles, the attack Iran claimed Thursday and nobody had confirmed. A tanker is hit by an unidentified projectile near Oman.

At Camp David, Trump says the US is planning new strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend'; only 28% of Americans approve of his handling of the five-month-old war. Brent back above $90, WTI near $84.67.
Trump says he's cancelled the planned strikes, citing an agreed framework on reopening the Strait of Hormuz after MBS and other regional leaders pressed for de-escalation over the weekend.

Iranian state media gives no sign it agrees to any deal; Fars news agency calls Trump's terms a 'wish list' and Iran's foreign ministry warns of a 'decisive response' to any future US-Israeli aggression.

Trump says a Hormuz deal is 'imminent' with talks resuming today, claiming Gulf allies asked him to hold off weekend strikes; Iranian semi-official media denies requesting any holdoff and denies agreeing to split control of the strait. Separately, Iran's FM says talks with Oman on a distinct new maritime route are in 'final stages' - though Iran's foreign ministry says that mechanism has nothing to do with whether the strait itself reopens. Oil eased on the deal optimism regardless.

Trump reverses to hostility, calling Iran's leadership 'unbelievably duplicitous' and declaring today its 'last chance' before 'decapitation,' after Iran says its only active negotiations are with Oman over a temporary shipping corridor, not direct talks with Washington. A cargo ship is reportedly hit by an unidentified projectile near the strait overnight.

Trump tells Fox News 'very good discussions' are underway with Iran and the strait will reopen 'very soon' or Iran gets hit 'very hard'; Iran continues to deny direct talks are happening, says Oman talks are in 'final stages.'

In a Fox interview, Trump says 'very good discussions' are underway and a deal could come as soon as Wednesday or Thursday; Iran and Oman report 'broad agreement' on a single shipping corridor, in final drafting; a Gulf official pegs real odds of a signed deal by Friday at only 50-50 since Iran's delegation excludes the IRGC; Houthis strike an eighth Saudi tanker near Yanbu in a separate campaign; oil dips toward $79 then bounces back over $80.

Iran shifts language to say the US is 'ready to return to commitments,' a modest move from flat denial, while still insisting no direct talks are underway and that full reopening depends on the US meeting its own conditions separately from the Oman shipping-route agreement.

Iranian state media reports the draft Iran-Oman plan now before Iran's parliament would bar ships linked to the US, Israel, and other 'hostile' countries from the strait, and charge other vessels fees up to 7% of cargo value, with 20% fines for violations. Washington rejects the terms almost immediately, saying any temporary routes must run without approvals, permissions, tolls, or charges, since the strait is an international waterway no party controls.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a NATO-style mutual-defense pact (the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement) at Al-Safa Palace Friday, read by analysts as a hedge against relying on US security guarantees mid-crisis. Trump said the war 'can't go much longer'; a CNN report said US Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine has privately signaled the US needs an 'off-ramp.' Iran's parliament has not confirmed passage of Thursday's disputed toll/ship-ban terms; Iran's deputy FM says the Oman shipping-corridor deal is close to finalized but reopening the strait itself still requires the US to separately meet Iran's conditions. Oil held roughly flat on the week, Brent near $83, WTI near $78.

Early Saturday, an ADNOC vessel is struck by a missile in the strait - no injuries, fire extinguished; the UAE calls it piracy by Iran's Revolutionary Guard and a violation of UN Security Council Resolution 2817. ADNOC says 15 of its vessels have been attacked since the war began, including three this week. Iran's Supreme National Security Council lays out its fullest public conditions yet for reopening: lift the US naval blockade and sanctions, withdraw regional forces, pay war reparations, release frozen Iranian assets. Iran's FM Araghchi says Oman talks are 'approaching final stages' but stresses that isn't the same as reopening the strait.

Houthi rebels claim a separate strike on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, a distinct campaign from Saturday's ADNOC tanker attack. Iran's public conditions for reopening remain unchanged from Saturday. US VP Vance says Washington is seeking to 'maximize' oil and gas flow through the strait.
Oil rises for a third straight session, Brent near $84, on fading hopes of a near-term Hormuz resolution; no new attacks reported overnight, but no softening in Iran's position either.

Oman and Iran continue describing the shipping-corridor talks as 'very close,' but a senior Iranian lawmaker says those talks are not about reopening the strait itself - that requires the US to end its blockade and leave the region first. No new attacks reported; oil extends its climb for a fourth session.

A US helicopter fired on a Panama-flagged ship Tuesday (per WSJ, citing a US official) after its crew allegedly ignored blockade-enforcement warnings - the first confirmed US strike on a vessel enforcing its own blockade; no casualties, fire extinguished. Trump claims 'complete control' of the strait and now demands reparations; Iran's Rezaei adds Gaza/Lebanon conditions to reopening terms. Iran and Oman say they've agreed on shipping-corridor coordinates, in final drafting.

A Houthi double-tap missile strike killed six aboard the Egyptian-owned, Tanzania-flagged cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab el-Mandeb - four crew and two rescuers, the first deadly Houthi strike there in a year. Separately, Reuters/Kpler data show Hormuz vessel traffic falling to a one-week low of eight ships (below a 10-day average of ~12), a fraction of the roughly 130-140 that transited daily before the blockade. Trump repeated his 'total control' claim on Truth Social; Iran's FM Araghchi warned of 'a bigger miscalculation' if Washington misjudges the situation. No new talks reported.

Traffic fell further to roughly 13 ships Tuesday, near a three-month low and about 90% below the pre-war daily average of 130, per Kpler data cited by CNBC. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority said flatly the strait 'remains blocked and will not be reopened until Iran's conditions are accepted,' directly disputing Trump's renewed 'total control' claim. No new talks or attacks reported.

The IEA's August Oil Market Report (published Aug 12) cut its 2026 global oil supply forecast by 4.3 million bpd and widened its projected Q3 deficit to 1.8 million bpd - a one-million-bpd downward revision from July - warning that 'the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupts international supply chains and curtails product availability.' No new attacks or talks reported since Thursday; Iran's position unchanged.

Iran struck two ADNOC (UAE state oil company) vessels transiting the strait Thursday evening; the UAE's Foreign Ministry called it 'piracy' and 'a direct threat to the stability of the region... and the global energy supply' in a formal statement the next day.

UKMTO reported a bulk carrier hit by an unidentified projectile in the strait; the crew was reported safe. Separately, in New York, Trump said that after 'defeating' Iran he would eventually declare the Strait of Hormuz 'a territory of the United States.'

Iranian officials rejected Trump's claim over the weekend - deputy FM Kazem Gharibabadi said 'the Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized with a tweet, an aircraft carrier, an executive order, or a campaign speech.' Strait traffic fell further, to roughly six ships a day (32 total transits over the weekend, 17 via Iran's own designated corridor) - even lower than earlier in the week. Iran and Oman continue describing a separate shipping-corridor arrangement as close to final, but no agreement on reopening the strait itself has been signed.

The 60-day US-Iran memorandum of understanding expires at midnight tonight, with both sides accusing each other of violations and neither showing real interest in extending it. Iran's FM Araghchi said Saturday no decision has been made on restarting talks with Washington. Trump's territorial claim, rejected by Iran over the weekend, has only hardened the freeze heading into tonight's deadline.

The 60-day Islamabad Memorandum formally expired Monday with neither side renewing it; Trump ruled out an extension, saying Tehran won't accept his terms. A ship's engine room was damaged and a crew member injured early Tuesday when an unidentified projectile struck a vessel transiting near Oman - the first confirmed attack since the MOU lapsed. Iranian military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari warned vessels attempting passage will find 'several beautiful holes in their hulls.' A WSJ report, citing Arab and Iranian officials, said Iran spent the 60-day window ramping up missile and drone production and elevating hardline figures rather than pursuing diplomacy. Brent crude rose and US stocks fell Monday on renewed war-reignition fears; Eurasia Group no longer expects a deal by September, pushing its timeline to year-end.

New Kpler shipping data shows over 80% of Strait transits in the past two weeks have shifted to the UN-authorized Omani route Iran opposes - versus almost none a month ago - and Iran can no longer collect tolls on strait traffic as it did in spring. Kpler's Homayoun Falakshahi: 'It increasingly looks like Iran has at least partially lost control of the strait.' Separately, the UAE said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles fired toward it from Iran Tuesday (Tehran denied responsibility), and Trump posted a graphic labeling the strait 'New US Territory' while threatening to bomb Oman if it interferes with US operations there. Oil ticked up to a multi-week high on the mixed signals.

Iran struck two more vessels in the strait Tuesday evening (one crew member injured) hours after the 60-day US-Iran memorandum formally lapsed. On Fox News, Trump escalated to an explicit on-camera threat to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of Iran-Oman shipping-corridor talks - a sharper version of his earlier social-media graphic. A CNN regional source says Iran and Oman could finalize that corridor agreement within days. UANI's Aug. 19 shipping count found only 13 identified vessels crossed in the prior 24 hours (plus 2 unidentified tankers running dark), underscoring how abnormal traffic remains even as the U.S. insists the strait is "open and operating." Oil extended its climb for a fourth straight session (Brent ~$92.36, WTI ~$85.63) on the mixed signals.

Trump pivoted from military threats to an explicit "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale" campaign against Iran (part of the administration's Operation Economic Fury pressure track since April), and the Treasury sanctioned Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy. Iran's deputy FM Kazem Gharibabadi called it a tell: "the military war didn't yield results, so now they've named the next failure economic war." No new vessel attack in the strait has been confirmed since the mid-August ADNOC cluster. Oil extended its climb for a fifth straight session (Brent $93.01, WTI $86.16).

Trump branded the pressure campaign an “economic D-Day,” and Treasury Secretary Bessent said he'll hold a press conference Monday, Aug. 24, to detail the new measures, including possible secondary sanctions on countries and companies doing business with Iran — a veiled threat aimed at China. China's foreign ministry rejected the pressure campaign outright (“sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution”) after Bessent publicly told Beijing to “get with the program”; China remains the largest buyer of Iranian crude via a shadow fleet. Iran's foreign ministry called the threat “a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism.” Brent held near a second straight ~6% weekly gain (~$94), WTI near $86.60; US retail gas prices are up nearly $1/gallon year-over-year.

Bessent said the US will impose "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran and explicitly called on China to cooperate, noting China bought over 80% of Iran's shipped oil in 2025. Washington has sanctioned only smaller Chinese "teapot" refineries so far, not major banks — reporting ties that restraint to Xi Jinping's state visit to the White House, now confirmed for Sept. 24 alongside the UN General Assembly. Monday's press conference is the next real test of how far the campaign goes.

Bessent's long-promised 'economic D-Day' press conference happens today at 2pm ET. Pre-conference reporting signals the sanctions finally reach past Iran's small teapot refineries toward the banks and foreign trade networks that actually move its oil — the exact restraint toward China that's held for weeks — though nothing is formally announced as of this morning. China's embassy again rejected the pressure campaign: 'sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem.'

Bessent held the long-promised press conference and unveiled 'Operation Economic Outcast,' expanding secondary sanctions to shipping, oil, crypto, gold, and aviation, and sanctioning roughly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels across multiple jurisdictions, including Chinese nationals. Asked directly whether Chinese banks would be targeted, Bessent said 'no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions' but gave no timeline for sanctioning them specifically -- real escalation in stated scope, still short of the direct hit on major Chinese financial institutions that would mark a genuine break with Beijing five weeks before Xi's White House visit.

Fresh analysis (CNN, CNBC) names China, India, Turkey, Iraq, and the UAE as the countries most exposed to Monday's sanctions expansion, with China -- roughly 9 of every 10 barrels of Iran's 2024 oil exports -- the only one that would matter. But experts are now openly skeptical Washington actually hits major Chinese banks: the US has 'never gone hard' on China sanctions historically, and Xi's White House visit is four weeks out.

Bessent drew the clearest conditional line yet: Chinese banks will be sanctioned if they 'facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money.' No major Chinese bank has actually been sanctioned, and Beijing continues buying over 80% of Iran's seaborne oil undisturbed -- a named threshold, still short of action, five weeks before Xi's White House visit.

As the war passes its six-month mark, Iran's IRGC claimed for the first time "decisive control" over the Strait of Hormuz -- directly contradicting Washington's own repeated "total control" claims -- and Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf publicly called Bessent's claim that the US guided 130 million barrels out of the Gulf in two weeks a lie. At least 6,000 sailors remain stranded aboard ships in the Gulf; no major Chinese bank has been sanctioned.

The month-long lull broke Sunday: the US struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island that IRGC forces had prepped to fire sea-mine rockets into the Strait -- the first American strike on Iran in over a month, days after the US Navy finished clearing mines from the Strait's own shipping lanes. Iran's Revolutionary Guard confirmed fighters and civilians killed or wounded and called the strike "a strategic and deadly mistake" it would punish.

Iran retaliated for Sunday's Larak Island strike with a coordinated missile-and-drone operation ("Punishment of the Aggressor") on Jordan's King Hussein and Al Azraq air bases, claiming heavy damage to infrastructure and aircraft positions; Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles. The UAE separately intercepted an Iranian drone approaching its airspace. Trump vowed to "hit them hard" and floated striking Kharg Island, Iran's main oil-export terminal -- a facility neither side has hit before. Brent jumped roughly 3% toward $91, WTI to about $86.50. Iran's president, speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, offered a conditional off-ramp: Iran would "immediately reciprocate" if the US returns to compliance with the lapsed Islamabad memorandum.

Trump's Sunday-night threat to strike Kharg Island turns out to have been an AI-generated fake video ("blown to smithereens"); Iran's national oil company called it "laughable" and a US official confirmed only Larak Island was ever hit. The real escalation landed elsewhere Tuesday: US strikes hit Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capability, and communications facilities near Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island, and Kerman province, after accusing the IRGC of trying to lay new mines in the Strait. One strike destroyed a home during a wedding in Kuhestak, Sirik county, killing at least five people including a child and wounding 63 (over half of them women and children). Iran retaliated with missiles and drones at regional targets; Trump vowed more strikes. Brent rose about 2% toward $95, a six-week high.

Iran's Red Crescent formally asked the ICC to investigate Tuesday's Sirik wedding strike as a possible war crime, naming four of the dead (a four-year-old and a 16-year-old among them) in its complaint -- though neither the US nor Iran has ratified the Rome Statute, so the court cannot compel either side's cooperation without a UN Security Council referral Washington can veto. Iran's army separately claimed Thursday it struck Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait and Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE overnight with missiles and drones; Kuwait's military said only that it was "confronting hostile" attacks, and neither Washington nor Kuwait has confirmed damage or casualties. Brent eased about 0.4% to roughly $95.25, snapping a three-day rally, as markets weighed the new claims against efforts to reopen the Strait.

Kuwait's army confirmed it intercepted a missile-and-drone attack from Iran, the first government confirmation (beyond Iran's own claim) of the Thursday overnight strikes. Iran's military separately says it also struck US bases/forces in Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq's Kurdistan region, widening its stated retaliation list. Oil surged on the confirmation: Brent +3.8% to $94.36, WTI +4.3% to its highest settle in over a month.

The Saudi-flagged tanker Sidr was struck by unidentified projectiles late Monday, August 31st, while approaching the strait; two of its 16 Filipino crew were killed, the 14 survivors taken to Oman for repatriation. Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the attack; Iran did not accept responsibility.

Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer; CENTCOM said both evaded the attack with no Americans harmed. The US retaliated by permanently disabling two Iranian crude carriers -- the Downy off Kharg Island and the Stark 1 near Jask -- and destroying a third, the Kylo, near the Gulf of Oman. It is the first direct US strike on Iran's own oil-export fleet, carrying out an earlier US warning to do exactly that if provoked.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it struck three oil tankers on an "unauthorized" Hormuz route plus three separate US-linked vessels, and claims a hit on a US unmanned military vessel that Washington hasn't confirmed. A US official described the tanker strikes as a deliberate "tanker for tanker" policy -- retaliation in kind for every future Iranian tanker attack, not a one-time response to Saturday's carrier incident. Brent extended its climb toward $97.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council head said Tehran plans to announce a maritime "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz, running from the line of the US naval blockade into the Persian Gulf; any vessel entering it to transit the strait would be placed on Iran's sanctions list. Iran also fired its Qassem Basir ballistic missile -- touted as manoeuvrable enough to evade missile defenses -- toward US warships, and its security council head threatened "new missiles" capable of hitting US warships and bases region-wide, plus a "more intense and more painful" retaliation. Strait traffic fell to its lowest level since May, about 10 ships a day per Kpler data. Brent traded near $97-98, a six-to-seven-week high.

CENTCOM says it destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers Tuesday after the IRGC targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over two days; the warship evaded both attacks and no Americans were harmed. Iran's Revolutionary Guard separately claims it captured a US Anduril-made Dive-LD unmanned underwater drone near the strait's entrance at dawn Tuesday; a Pentagon spokesperson says the drone had malfunctioned more than a day earlier and carried no classified sonar or radar equipment. Iran's IRGC claims it retaliated by striking two US-linked vessels and eight oil tankers -- "10 offending vessels" -- in the Gulf. Brent held near a seven-week high around $97.

Iran retaliated for Tuesday's tanker strikes with roughly twenty ballistic missiles at Jordan's Al Azraq air base (Jordan says it intercepted eighteen, two fell in unpopulated areas, no casualties) and claimed a separate ten-vessel strike wave near Hormuz -- the largest declared wave of shipping attacks since the six-month war began -- reportedly killing one seafarer and leaving another missing. Brent crude broke above $100 for the first time in six weeks, closing Wednesday at $101.21 (WTI $96.05), the highest settle since May. Iran's planned exclusion zone remains undeclared.

Brent closed Thursday at $107.63 (+5.94%), briefly touching $108 intraday, the highest level in four months, as no new strikes were reported since Wednesday's Jordan/Hormuz wave. Trump warned Iran over renewed construction activity at its "Pickaxe Mountain" nuclear site, saying the US "may" strike it soon. Separately, Oman is convening Iran's foreign minister and all six Gulf Cooperation Council states in Salalah on Monday, September 14 -- the first senior Iran-Gulf meeting since the war began -- to discuss a temporary arrangement for reopening the Strait; diplomats caution any real reopening still needs US sign-off.

Brent fell 2.8% Friday to $104.61 after Iran's state media confirmed it will meet all six GCC states and Iraq in Salalah, Oman on Monday, September 14 -- the first senior Iran-Gulf sit-down since the war began, aimed at temporary shipping-corridor and mine-clearance arrangements rather than a full reopening. No new strikes reported since Thursday.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said it will not attend Monday's Salalah meeting, citing its policy of not joining any collective session with Iran before diplomatic relations (severed in 2016) are restored; it also called for the strait to reopen without discrimination, fees, or permits. The other five GCC states, Iraq, and Iran are still expected to attend.

Catch-up: drone strikes launched from Iraqi territory hit Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline near Riyadh and Medina, causing fires and injuries. Saudi Arabia shut the pipeline as a precaution, temporarily losing the roughly 5 million bpd Red Sea rerouting alternative it had been using to bypass the blocked strait; Riyadh said it would not retaliate for now, at Baghdad's request.

Iranian state media claimed an Iranian commercial vessel was struck late Saturday near Qeshm Island, killing one and injuring four -- the latest in the pattern of unclaimed and claimed vessel attacks inside the strait.

Oman postponed Monday's Salalah meeting indefinitely -- not merely the reduced, Bahrain-minus version reported Saturday, but the meeting entirely -- citing a need for more 'conducive' conditions after the Qeshm strike and the Saudi pipeline attack. Brent surged to roughly $107 Monday (session range $106-108), its highest level of the war, up from Friday's $104.61 close.

Reporting reveals Saudi Arabia, not just Oman's own judgment, requested Monday's Salalah postponement -- objecting to proposed changes in the Iran-Oman shipping-corridor framework and citing frustration with continued Houthi attacks on Saudi territory. Separately, Iran's security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei says Tehran will hold no talks with Washington until Iran's own conditions are met. Brent held near $107.46 Tuesday.

Monday's Salalah summit -- the first planned Iran-Gulf sit-down of the war -- was postponed indefinitely rather than merely reduced, with no new date set. Trackers disagree sharply on how blocked Hormuz actually is right now: one count puts Monday's commercial traffic as low as four vessels (vs. a ~125/day pre-war average), while satellite imagery from the same day shows some bidirectional daytime supertanker movement. Brent eased from Tuesday's ~$109 close into the $104-106 range Thursday morning.

Trump told Axios he's nearing a 'big decision' on Iran, framed explicitly as whether to 'annihilate' the regime, citing 18 US service members killed, 3,000+ Iranians dead, and roughly $38B in war costs. He separately claimed direct contact with Tehran and said the war is 'hopefully toward the end' -- which Iranian officials flatly dispute; security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei says no negotiation until the US fully returns to the lapsed Islamabad memorandum. Trump plans to meet Gulf Cooperation Council leaders on the UN General Assembly sidelines in New York around September 22 for 'day-after' planning; Iran's FM Araghchi made his second Beijing trip of the war, meeting China's Wang Yi. Saudi Aramco says it's restoring roughly half its drone-damaged East-West pipeline's capacity within days (full within about six weeks), one factor easing Brent toward the low $100s. Iran's IRGC separately claims, unconfirmed, that it struck a Togo-flagged tanker in the strait overnight.

threads.title: Federal Reserve rate path
threads.current_state: Wednesday's hawkish hike triggered a selloff that reversed hard Thursday: stocks are up roughly 1.1-1.7%, the 10-year has eased to about 4.95%, and October meeting odds have flipped toward a hold (CME FedWatch ~59-60% hold vs ~40% hike) -- a real gap against the Fed's own dot plot, where 16 of 18 officials still see at least one more 2026 hike. Next meeting: October 27-28.

timeline.summary: Hike odds rising toward 46%; BofA sees three hikes by December.
Fed week arrives; positioning visible in Friday's chip-led selloff.
Hike odds collapse to 13.3% (86.7% hold) amid Iran-driven oil shock; 10Y ticks up to 4.59%.
Hike odds tick back up to 16.6% as oil keeps climbing; stocks rally anyway on chip earnings; June CPI confirmed at 3.5%.
Wednesday's close confirmed as a reversal of Tuesday's rally (S&P -0.14%, Nasdaq -0.56%); 10Y up to 4.66%.
Sharp selloff on oil breaking $100 plus Tesla/Alphabet earnings: S&P -1.21%, Nasdaq -2.15%; 10Y to 4.70%, highest since Jan 2025; hike odds more than double to roughly 36.5%.
Friday's close: S&P +0.05% to 7,412, Nasdaq -0.64% to 24,976 on continued tech weakness, 10Y flat at 4.69%; hike odds ease slightly to about 34% (66% hold) heading into the weekend.
Monday premarket: futures jump (Dow/S&P +0.8%, Nasdaq +1.6%) as oil craters; 10Y eases to about 4.64%; hike odds around 35% for Wednesday, September odds climb to about 82%.

FOMC's two-day meeting formally opens; Monday's close came in mixed rather than the rally premarket implied (S&P +0.02% to 7,413.18, Nasdaq -0.18% to 24,932.08); the 10Y eases further to about 4.62% Tuesday; hike odds hold in the mid-to-high 30s.

Decision due today at 2 PM ET; hike odds climb further to about 38%; Tuesday's close was essentially flat (S&P +0.02% to 7,413.18, Nasdaq -0.22% to 24,876.91), 10Y held near a one-week low at 4.64%; overnight Iran escalation adds a fresh input hours before the vote.

FOMC votes 9-3 to hold at 3.50-3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan dissent in favor of a hike. Market reads the hold as hawkish-in-disguise: S&P -1.52% to 7,316.15, Nasdaq -1.74% to 24,442.94, 10Y up to roughly 4.66%.

Meta misses Q2 earnings on legal/severance charges and guides to $130-145B in AI capex this year; shares fall nearly 10%, adding a second worry to the Fed-driven selloff even as broader futures point to a Thursday bounce.
Thursday morning: 10Y holds near 4.68%, 30Y hits roughly 5.24% (a multidecade high); hike odds for the next meeting jump to about 54% from 38% pre-decision, even as equity futures rebound.

Thursday's close: S&P +1.7% to 7,437.64, Nasdaq +2.8% to 25,122.18, Microsoft up about 15% on AI earnings - nearly erasing the post-Fed selloff. The 10-year still rose 8bp to 4.704%, its highest close of the stretch.

Friday's close: S&P +0.7% to 7,489.72, Nasdaq +1% to 25,373.85, Amazon up ~13% (its biggest single-day gain in over a decade) on an earnings beat - the Dow's fourth straight winning month. The 10-year topped 4.70% for the first time since January 2025; the 30-year hit its highest since 2007.
Prediction markets price roughly 53% odds of a September 25bp hike, versus ~32% implied by SOFR futures. No jobs report today; the next release, for July, is pushed to Friday, August 7.

Markets closed for the weekend. Kalshi prices roughly 57% odds of a September hike, 42% hold, 2% cut - up from Polymarket's 53% Friday. Economists expect Friday's jobs report to show 100,000-130,000 jobs added in July and unemployment holding at 4.2%.

Markets reopen with premarket futures pointing higher (S&P and Nasdaq both roughly +0.4-0.6%). September hike odds keep drifting hawkish but diverge sharply by platform - Kalshi's own tracker near the mid-50s%, other aggregators as high as the low-to-mid 60s% - ahead of Friday's jobs report and this week's ISM PMI releases.

Monday's confirmed close sets records: S&P +1.48% to 7,600.50 (first close above 7,600), Nasdaq +2.13% to 25,913.90, Dow +693 points to 53,178, on Iran diplomacy optimism (since reversed) and a Big Tech rally - Amazon topped a $3 trillion market cap. September hike odds diverge further than ever: CME's FedWatch near 81-82%, Kalshi near 54%.

Tuesday's confirmed close: S&P +1.79% to 7,737, Dow +907 points to a first-ever close above 54,000, Nasdaq +2.59% to 26,585. September hike odds converge to near-agreement - CME's FedWatch near 55.9%, Kalshi near 54% - down from Monday's near-30-point spread.

Wednesday's confirmed close splits: Dow sets a new record at 54,349.12 (+0.5%), S&P falls 0.2% to 7,723.55, Nasdaq falls 0.8% to 26,363.44 on earnings-driven selling (SpaceX, AMD); 10-year holds flat near 4.62%. Minneapolis Fed's Kashkari says publicly 'now is the time' to raise rates; September hike odds drift higher again across trackers, though the precise number is unsettled (roughly mid-50s to low-60s%).
Thursday premarket futures flat to slightly higher ahead of Friday's July jobs report, still scheduled for 8:30am ET; consensus expects payrolls around +75-120K and unemployment holding near 4.2%.

Thursday's confirmed close fell across the board: S&P -0.18% to 7,709.96, Nasdaq -0.06% to 26,348.35, Dow -464.02 points (-0.85%) to 53,885, snapping its record streak. 10-year held near 4.61%, oil rose on stalled Hormuz talks. September hike odds kept climbing, roughly high-50s to mid-60s%. Friday's jobs report, due 8:30am ET, remains the key input ahead of the Sept 16 FOMC meeting.

Friday's confirmed close: S&P +0.62% to a record 7,757.64, Nasdaq +1.3% to a record 26,690.62, Dow +0.28% to 54,036.93 - second straight winning week, S&P's best week since April. The 10-year eased to roughly 4.60%. July payrolls fell 23,000 (vs. roughly +80,000 expected), unemployment eased to 4.1% on falling participation, and May/June were revised down a combined 103,000. September hike odds reversed sharply toward a hold - CME FedWatch near 60%, Kalshi near 65% - a flip from the climbing-hike narrative that had run all week. Next catalyst: July CPI, due August 12.

Monday premarket: S&P futures near 7,786, Nasdaq 100 futures up roughly 60 points, Dow futures reportedly softer as oil extends its climb on stalled Hormuz diplomacy. Odds trackers little changed from Friday - CME ~55-60% hold, Kalshi 65% hold/33% hike/2% cut, Polymarket ~63% no-change. July CPI, due Wednesday, August 12, is the next real catalyst.

Monday's confirmed close: S&P -0.06% to 7,753.20, Nasdaq -0.32% to 26,605.31, 10-year up 6bp to 4.71% - highest close of the stretch - as oil climbed further and Fed officials leaned hawkish on inflation risk. CME FedWatch's September hike odds jumped to 44.4% from Friday's low-30s%. July CPI, due tomorrow at 8:30am ET, is the decisive input.

July CPI released: headline steady at 2.7% y/y (+0.2% m/m), core jumps to 3.1% y/y (+0.32% m/m), highest since February and above ~2.5% consensus, on core services strength and tariff pass-through. Tuesday's confirmed close: S&P -0.32% to 7,728.20, Nasdaq -0.60% to 26,445.45, 10Y up to 4.73%. Pre-print, September hike/hold odds were close to even on CME FedWatch; post-print move not yet confirmed.

Settled figures across CNBC, NBC News, Fox Business, and others confirm July CPI actually came in cool, not hot: headline +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y (down from 3.5% in June); core +0.2% m/m, 2.5% y/y (down from 2.6%) - both right on Dow Jones consensus, largely on energy prices down 7% from their May peak. This reverses the 'hot core, 3.1%' read that circulated in early Tuesday-night/Wednesday-morning wires (FXStreet) and drove yesterday's edition. Wednesday's confirmed close: S&P +0.3% to 7,748.50, Nasdaq +0.5% to 26,588.49 on AI-capex strength, Dow roughly flat; 10-year eased to 4.68% from Tuesday's 4.73%. September hike odds fell to roughly 40-42% (hold near 58-60%) on CME FedWatch, reversing the hawkish drift of the prior week.

July PPI (BLS) came in flat month-over-month vs. +0.2% expected, a second straight soft inflation print. CME FedWatch's September hike odds fell further to roughly 32% (from 40-42% Wednesday), with some trackers now pricing real odds of a cut rather than a hold. S&P 500 closed at a fresh record, 7,798.99 (+0.7%); Nasdaq also closed at a record, 26,803.03 (+0.81%); 10-year eased to 4.65%.

Friday's preliminary August consumer sentiment fell to 51.0 (vs. 54.5 expected, down from July's 55.2 per the University of Michigan) - inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. S&P 500 -0.17% to 7,786, Nasdaq -0.28% to 26,729, Dow -0.20% to 53,732, ending the two-day record streak; 10-year ticked up to roughly 4.69% from Thursday's 4.65%. S&P still closed a third straight winning week. September hike odds remain near Thursday's ~32% CME FedWatch reading; no fresh print confirmed Friday.

Fuller picture of Friday's slide: July retail sales fell 0.6% - the first monthly drop in nine months - compounding the weak consumer-sentiment miss. September hike odds on CME FedWatch fell to roughly 29-31% by Friday's close, down from about 44% a week earlier and the lowest reading of the week; some trackers now price real odds of a hold or even a cut. The S&P still closed its third straight winning week.

No economic data released over the weekend; September hike odds hold near Friday's close of roughly 30-31% (about 69% odds of a hold). No major releases are scheduled before the September 16 FOMC meeting, which remains the next real catalyst.

Stocks fell and Treasury yields rose Monday as Hormuz risk resurfaced - S&P 500 -0.52% to 7,745.06, Nasdaq -0.32% to 26,644.91, 10-year near 4.68%. September hike odds hold at the most recently confirmed reading of roughly 69% for a hold (~30% hike), from Thursday Aug 14 - no fresher print has surfaced since. Home Depot reports Q2 earnings today, opening a retail-earnings week (Target/Lowe's Wednesday, Walmart Thursday) that will be read as a consumer-spending signal against the oil-price backdrop.

Tuesday's confirmed close: S&P 500 -0.69% to 7,691.76, Nasdaq -1.33% to 26,289.71 (chip-led selloff), Dow -0.2%; 10-year up to 4.72%, its highest close of the stretch, as oil rose on Trump's Oman threat. Home Depot beat Q2 estimates (revenue +5.7% YoY to $47.9B, comps +1.7%) even while calling the housing market 'frozen'; Target, Lowe's, TJX, and Estee Lauder report today. September hike odds little changed at roughly 68% hold / 32% hike.

Wednesday's confirmed close: S&P +0.21% to 7,707.98, Dow +119.65 points to 53,463.05, Nasdaq +0.16% to 26,331.09 - snapping the three-day losing streak after Treasury announced it would double its long-dated debt buyback, easing the 10-year to roughly 4.65% from Tuesday's 4.72%. Tuesday's retail earnings gave a mixed consumer read: Target beat (comps +3.8% vs. 2.4% expected, raised FY guidance) but its stock slipped; TJX beat but fell 4.7% on light Q3 guidance; Lowe's fell on cautious full-year guidance citing DIY spending pressure; Estee Lauder jumped 8% on a genuine beat-and-raise. Walmart reports before today's open - the week's clearest read yet on U.S. household spending. September FOMC hold odds sit near 65% (35% hike), essentially unchanged.

Thursday's confirmed close reversed Wednesday's rally: S&P -0.87% to 7,641.16, Dow -1.32% (-703.84 pts) to 52,759.21, Nasdaq -1.0% to 26,067.17; the 10-year rose back to roughly 4.70% from Wednesday's 4.65%. Walmart beat on revenue ($187.94B) and adjusted EPS ($0.81) but posted US comp-sales growth of just 2.6% - the slowest in six years - and guided Q3 EPS softly to $0.62-0.64; the stock fell 9.15%, its worst day in over four years, and was the single biggest drag on the market. September FOMC hold odds held roughly steady at 65-68% (32-35% hike).

Friday's confirmed close rebounded across the board: S&P +0.43% to 7,674.37, Dow +0.98% (+517.80 pts) to 53,277.01, Nasdaq +0.43% to 26,180.45, led less by any economic data than by a crypto rally (bitcoin +7% to roughly $76,900, +22% on the week) that lifted Robinhood and Coinbase alongside the broader tape. The 10-year held steady near 4.71%. Despite the bounce, all three indices still closed lower for the week (S&P -1.4%, Nasdaq -2.1%, Dow -0.9%) after Thursday's Walmart-driven selloff. September FOMC hold odds sit near 68% (32% hike) on CME FedWatch, essentially unchanged from Thursday — new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh (confirmed May 13, sworn in May 22) delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote as chair next Friday, Aug. 28.

Monday premarket points softer: Dow futures down about 11 points, S&P and Nasdaq-100 futures off 0.1% and 0.5%, tech leading declines (XLK -1%) after last week's second straight losing week for the Dow. September FOMC hold odds essentially unchanged near 68%. The week ahead: Nvidia earnings and the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, which opens Thursday Aug. 27 with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first keynote as chair Friday at 10am ET — 19 days before the Sept. 16 decision.

Monday's confirmed close came in more uneven than the premarket drift suggested: S&P 500 -0.28% to 7,652.86, Nasdaq -0.76% to 25,980.19 on chip-sector weakness (Nvidia -2.91%, SanDisk -6.45%) ahead of Wednesday's earnings, while the Dow actually gained 0.26% (+140.15 points) to 53,417.16. Tuesday premarket points modestly higher (S&P futures +0.12%, Nasdaq 100 futures +0.37%). Wednesday now confirmed as a double-header: July's PCE inflation report (the Fed's preferred gauge) at 8:30am ET, and Nvidia earnings after the close -- both ahead of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as chair, Friday at 10am ET, 19 days before the Sept. 16 decision. CME FedWatch September hold odds sit near 68-70%.

Tuesday's confirmed close reversed Monday's chip-led split: S&P +0.32% to 7,677.28, Nasdaq +0.66% to 26,151.30, Dow +0.30% (+160 pts) to 53,579.94, closing in on the S&P's record high as oil fell and the 10-year eased to 4.66%. September FOMC odds little changed (~70% hold, ~30% hike). Wednesday is the week's real test: July PCE (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge) lands at 8:30am ET, and Nvidia reports after the close (~4:20-4:30pm ET) -- both ahead of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Friday Jackson Hole keynote.

Wednesday's confirmed close came in essentially flat-to-down, not the rally Tuesday implied: S&P -0.02% to 7,675.70, Nasdaq -0.08% to 26,130.20, Dow -0.21% (-113.52 pts) to 53,463.88, 10-year easing slightly to 4.65%. July PCE landed mixed: headline 3.7% y/y (vs. 3.6% expected, hotter), core -- the Fed's real focus -- exactly in line at 0.2% m/m and 3.3% y/y; consumer spending was flat, a sharp slowdown from June's 0.4% gain.

Nvidia reported after Wednesday's close: $96.2B revenue (+106% y/y, vs. $92.2B expected) and $2.22 non-GAAP EPS (vs. $2.09 expected), with Amazon confirming a 2-million-GPU order. The stock is up roughly 6% in Thursday's premarket, lifting S&P futures +0.5% and Nasdaq-100 futures +1% as the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium opens today in Wyoming -- Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first keynote as chair tomorrow, Friday, at 10am ET. September FOMC odds little changed (~68-70% hold).

Thursday's confirmed close: Nvidia finished up 9.1% -- the second-biggest single-day market-cap gain by any stock in history, adding $442B -- lifting the S&P 500 0.72% to 7,731 and the Nasdaq 1.57% to 26,541; the Dow added 0.2% to 53,569.44. The 10-year rose to roughly 4.68%. September hike odds drifted hawkish to roughly 34-36% (64-66% hold) on CME FedWatch, up from Wednesday's ~30-32%, as the Jackson Hole Symposium's second day brings Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first keynote as chair at 10am ET -- the week's last real catalyst before the Sept. 16 decision.

Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as chair read as genuinely hawkish -- inflation running too high, price stability his 'predominant focus' -- and September hike odds on CME FedWatch jumped to roughly 56-57% (Kalshi 48%, Polymarket 49%), from 34-36% pre-speech. Friday's confirmed close: S&P -0.25% to 7,711, Nasdaq -0.52% to 26,402, Dow roughly flat at 53,560; all three still closed a winning week. The 10-year held near 4.67%.

Fuller weekend read of Friday's keynote surfaces Warsh's real break from precedent: he explicitly rejected giving forward guidance, telling Jackson Hole "we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade," and calling a "quieter Fed" better able to meet its objectives -- even as most investors now price a September hike. Monday's premarket softened further after the US struck Iran's Larak Island overnight, the first US-Iran military action in a month; September hike odds hold near Friday's 56-57% on CME FedWatch.

Warsh reiterated his hawkish line in G20 remarks Monday, arguing the low-inflation era is over and price stability remains the Fed's dominant focus. September hike odds held near Friday's 56-57% (CME FedWatch) into Tuesday morning, with markets now watching two real catalysts before the Sept. 16 decision: today's ISM Manufacturing PMI (10am ET) and Friday's August jobs report (8:30am ET) -- the last major print before the FOMC's blackout period begins Saturday, Sept. 5.

August's ISM Manufacturing PMI came in at 54.6, below the 55.2 consensus and down from July's 55.6 -- an eighth straight month of expansion but clearly decelerating, normally a dovish signal. CME FedWatch's September hike odds moved the opposite direction anyway, firming to roughly 66% (from 56-57% Friday) as markets continued repricing Warsh's hawkish G20/Jackson Hole framing over the incoming data itself. Tuesday's close: S&P 500 -0.71% to 7,631.47, Nasdaq -1.03% to 26,099.77, both giving back more of August's gains as oil climbed on the Iran strikes; the 10-year rose to about 4.80%, its highest close of the stretch.

Wednesday's confirmed close: S&P 500 +0.46% to 7,666.60, Nasdaq +0.45% to 26,217.83, both recovering part of Tuesday's slide as Treasury yields paused their climb; the 10-year eased to roughly 4.79% from Tuesday's 4.80%, a session after touching its highest close since October 2023. September hike odds held essentially unchanged near 65-66% on CME FedWatch. Friday's August jobs report, 8:30am ET, is now the last data point before the FOMC's blackout period begins Saturday, September 5 -- the only thing left that can move the odds before the Sept. 16 decision.

Governor Christopher Waller said he would be inclined to support holding the federal funds rate at its current setting if inflation data over the next two weeks continues showing progress toward 2%, while reserving the right to change course. CME FedWatch September hike odds fell about twelve points to roughly 55% from 66%. Stocks turned higher (S&P +0.7%, Nasdaq +0.9%, Dow +450) and the 10-year eased to about 4.76% from 4.79%. Initial jobless claims rose to 206,000 (consensus 205,000), continuing claims to 1.78 million; Wednesday's ADP showed private payrolls up 38,000 versus 47,000 expected.

CORRECTION. An earlier entry for this date reported August payrolls at +22,000 with unemployment at 4.3 percent. Those figures were wrong and have been removed. BLS USDL-26-1435 (8:30am ET Sept 4) reports payrolls +162,000 vs consensus near 53,000-56,000, unemployment unchanged at 4.1 percent, average hourly earnings +3.1 percent y/y, June revised up to +31,000 and July revised up from -23,000 to +21,000 (combined +55,000). CME FedWatch put a September quarter-point hike near 60 percent after the print; two-year 4.37 percent, ten-year 4.78 percent. Blackout begins Saturday.

The FOMC's pre-meeting blackout formally begins today. Friday's confirmed close: S&P 500 -0.38% to 7,718.60, Nasdaq -0.29% to 26,506.99; the 10-year held in a 4.76-4.78% range depending on source. August CPI is now dated: Friday, September 11 at 8:30am ET, the last data the committee sees before the September 16 decision. CME FedWatch read a September hike near 60% right after Friday's jobs print, with some trackers showing readings as high as 66%.
No new data over the weekend; the blackout enters its second week with nothing to move the odds until August CPI, due Friday, September 11 at 8:30am ET.

Labor Day: US markets closed, blackout holds. CME FedWatch odds unchanged near 60% for a September hike since Friday's post-jobs read; nothing will move until August CPI, Friday September 11 at 8:30am ET.

Markets reopen after Labor Day. CME FedWatch's September hike odds sit near 58-59%, essentially unchanged from Friday's ~60% read. Friday's confirmed close remains the last print: S&P 500 -0.38% to 7,718.60, Nasdaq -0.29% to 26,506.99, the 10-year near 4.78-4.79%. August CPI, Friday September 11 at 8:30am ET, remains the last input before the September 16 decision.

Tuesday's confirmed close: S&P 500 -0.58% to 7,673.52, Nasdaq -0.32% to 26,421.41, Dow -628.18 points (-1.18%) to 52,786.07 -- the week's worst session, as investors weighed the fresh Hormuz escalation (five Iranian tankers destroyed, a disputed US drone capture) against Friday's looming CPI. The 10-year held near 4.79%. September hike odds on CME FedWatch sit roughly 58-60%, essentially unchanged, with August CPI on Friday, September 11 at 8:30am ET still the last input before the September 16 decision.

Wednesday's confirmed close: S&P 500 -0.48% to 7,636.36, Nasdaq -0.64% to 26,253.34, Dow -405.41 (-0.77%) to 52,380.66, Russell 2000 -1.30%. The 10-year rose to roughly 4.83-4.85%, its highest close since October 2023, on fiscal worries and heavy AI-sector debt issuance. CME FedWatch's September hike odds ranged 56-66% across trackers this week -- an unusually wide, fast-moving spread tied to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole remarks. August CPI, Friday September 11 at 8:30am ET, remains the deciding input.

A hot August PPI print pushed CME FedWatch's September 16 hike odds to roughly 70%, from 56-66% Wednesday and 44% a week earlier. Thursday's confirmed close: S&P 500 -0.6% to 7,591.70, Dow -0.6% to 52,064.10, Nasdaq -0.7% to 26,081.72, a fourth straight losing session; the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.95%, its highest close since October 2023, on the hot PPI and Brent's climb toward $108. August CPI -- the last input before Wednesday's decision -- released this morning at 8:30am ET; settled figures and market reaction were not yet independently confirmed through primary sources as this edition went to print.

August CPI landed at 8:30am as expected -- headline +0.4% m/m (3.4% y/y), core +0.3% m/m (2.4% y/y, the lowest annual core reading in over five years) -- but far from reassuring markets on a hold: CME FedWatch odds for the September 16 hike jumped further, to roughly 85-90%, since an in-line-but-not-soft print removed the last real chance of a surprise. Stocks rallied anyway (S&P +0.9% to 7,656.98, Dow +1% to 52,573.29, Nasdaq +1% to 26,333.04) as Brent's pullback eased inflation-input fears; the 10-year closed at 4.96%, a hair from 5%.

Monday premarket: S&P 500 futures -0.5%, Nasdaq-100 futures -1.2% on oil's surge past $106 (Salalah postponement, Houthi Red Sea gains, Saudi pipeline shutdown) compounded by AI-industry warnings of a development slowdown; hike odds hold near 85-90% ahead of Wednesday's decision and dot plot.

The 10-year Treasury rose intraday to 5.01% Monday -- matching October 2023's brief high and the highest level since 2007 -- before easing to close near 4.987%. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Dow all confirmed Monday's premarket weakness at the close (S&P -0.46% to 7,621.54, Nasdaq -0.56% to 26,186.41, Dow -0.29% to 52,421). CME FedWatch hike odds hold near 88-91%, though Kalshi (57%) and Polymarket (49%) show real disagreement ahead of Wednesday's decision.

Tuesday's close: 10-year Treasury finished at ~5.00% (its first actual close at that level since 2007) after touching 5.04% intraday; S&P/Nasdaq/Dow all fell a second straight session. CME FedWatch hike odds for today's 2pm ET decision rose to ~93%; Polymarket converged to ~89% (from 49% Friday). Brent near $109, +3.34% Tuesday.

The FOMC voted 12-0 Wednesday to raise the target range 25bp to 3.75%-4.00%, the first hike since 2023. The new dot plot shows 16 of 18 officials expecting at least one more hike this year (4 see two), median funds rate projected at 4.10% through all of 2027 with no cuts penciled in. Stocks fell despite the hike being priced above 90%: Dow -631pts (-1.21%) to 51,461.90, S&P -0.45% to 7,551.81, Nasdaq roughly flat (-0.01%) to 25,978.42. The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.016%, pushing past Tuesday's 5.00% close.

Markets rebounded Thursday from Wednesday's hawkish-hike selloff: the S&P 500 rose roughly 1.1-1.2% to about 7,638, the Nasdaq gained roughly 1.6-1.7% to about 26,418, and the 10-year eased about 6bp to roughly 4.95% from Wednesday's 5.016% close. October 27-28 odds now lean toward a hold -- CME FedWatch near 59-60% hold vs roughly 40% hike, Polymarket close to even -- even though the Fed's own dot plot still points to at least one more 2026 hike.

threads.title: Marlins wild card race
threads.current_state: Resolved: the Marlins closed their season with a 6-4 win over the Dodgers Sunday, finishing outside the NL wild-card picture. A genuinely well-played final week -- two wins over a playoff-bound Dodgers team -- closes out a season that was mathematically over well before it ended.

timeline.summary: Hit the break 52-45, holding WC pole position.
Swept in Milwaukee; three straight losses out of the break.
Lost Astros opener; Meyer placed on IL with neck strain; streak at seven.
Lost again, confirmed final Houston 5, Miami 3; streak reaches eight straight, longest since April 2024.
Alcantara's start ends in a 5-2 loss; Houston completes the sweep; streak reaches nine straight.
Lost to the Padres 4-2 Friday night, the 10th straight loss, first time since June 2011; Miami falls to 52-52, first .500 record since June 19.
Lost again, 7-2, Ty France driving in three for San Diego; the streak reaches 11, tying the franchise record last matched in June 2011.

Lost Sunday 5-3 to San Diego, Machado and Merrill homering in the eighth to erase a three-run deficit; the streak reaches 12, an outright franchise record. Miami falls to 52-53, its first losing record since mid-June.

Miami beats the Phillies 8-7 on a walk-off single by Griffin Conine after Philadelphia's closer loaded the bases in the ninth, ending the losing streak at 12 - the Marlins' first win since July 9. Record moves to 53-53.

Correction: the 8-7 walk-off was Monday's game, not Tuesday's. Tuesday was a separate 1-0 win, Alcantara's major-league-leading 16th quality start with a Kyle Stowers homer; Miami has won two straight and stands 54-54 ahead of today's series finale.
Trade deadline plan surfaces: Miami will keep Alcantara, Eury Perez, Max Meyer, and Joe Mack, but is willing to take calls on Xavier Edwards, Otto Lopez, Liam Hicks, and Heriberto Hernandez.

Down 6-0, Miami completes the sweep of the Phillies with an 8-6 win, its biggest comeback of the season; Conine's go-ahead pinch-hit homer and two RBIs each from Lopez, Hernandez, and Edwards. Miami improves to 55-54, three straight wins, opening at the Mets next.

Deadline plan detail expands: Miami could also field calls on veteran relievers 31 or older - Anthony Bender, Michael Petersen, Lake Bachar, and John King - alongside the position-player names already in play, four days before the August 3 deadline.
Mets beat Miami 4-2 on Luis Robert Jr.'s eighth-inning two-run single, snapping Miami's three-game winning streak.

Boston reportedly weighs a bigger package for Otto Lopez that could include catcher Liam Hicks, after a wrist injury sidelines Red Sox infielder Curtis Mead for 6-8 weeks; Miami remains in a 'listening' stage rather than committed to a deal, three days before the deadline.
Miami beats the Mets 5-2, improving to 56-55 and staying in wild-card contention.

The Guardians join Boston in showing interest in Otto Lopez; insider Jon Morosi puts the odds of a trade at roughly 25%, with most signals pointing toward Miami keeping him, two days before the deadline.
Miami beats the Mets again, 6-2, on homers from Javier Sanoja and Griffin Conine - its sixth win in seven games, one day before the deadline.

Red Sox-Marlins talks on Otto Lopez are reportedly 'dead' - Miami's asking price, headlined by an elite prospect, was more than Boston would pay. The Guardians remain in the market but face a similarly steep price. The deadline hits 6pm ET today with no trade reported.

The 6pm deadline passed with Lopez staying in Miami. The Marlins instead made four smaller trades: Liam Hicks to Tampa Bay, Braxton Garrett to the Cubs, Lake Bachar to Pittsburgh, and acquired reliever Victor Vodnik from Colorado for infielder Connor Norby and pitcher Aiden May.

Atlanta shuts out Miami 4-0 in the Marlins' first game since the deadline passed with Lopez staying; Miami remains outside a wild-card spot. The organization introduces the prospects acquired in its four deadline trades.

Atlanta's Bryce Elder holds Miami to one hit over seven innings in a 4-1 win, Miami's second straight loss since the deadline. Marlins fall to 58-56, roughly two and a half games behind Arizona for the final NL wild-card spot, with the Cubs and Phillies further ahead. Miami recalled catcher Agustin Ramirez and activated reliever Josh Ekness off the 60-day IL.

Atlanta completes the sweep 11-3 - Acuna hits two home runs and Olson adds one, the Braves' eighth straight win. Miami falls to 58-57, now 3.0 games back in the wild-card race, on the cutline but outside the three spots held by the Cubs, Diamondbacks, and Phillies.

The Angels beat Miami 4-3 Friday at loanDepot Park - Mike Trout and Nolan Schanuel both homered. Marlins fall to 58-58, still roughly 3.0 games back of the final NL wild-card spot. Miami hosts the Angels again Saturday at 4:10pm with Sandy Alcantara starting.
Miami shuts out the Angels 7-0 Saturday at loanDepot Park, improving to 59-58 and pulling to roughly 2.5-3.0 games back of the final wild-card spot. Sunday's 1:40pm rubber match decides the series.

Miami routs the Angels 12-3 Sunday, taking the series and improving to 60-58, roughly two games back of a wild-card spot (Cubs 68-50; Diamondbacks and Phillies both 62-56). Kyle Stowers, who opened the season on the IL with a hamstring strain, leaves the game with left hamstring discomfort after a two-run single.
Miami is off Monday; next hosts Pittsburgh Tuesday-Wednesday, August 11-12. Stowers' availability for the series opener is unconfirmed.

Stowers underwent an MRI Monday; no result is public yet. Miami hosts Pittsburgh tonight at loanDepot Park, Eury Perez (5-9, 3.61) against Paul Skenes (9-10, 3.96), who has a 5.20 ERA over his last 15 starts.

Stowers placed on the 10-day IL, retroactive to Aug 10, with a Grade 1 left hamstring strain - his second hamstring IL stint this season - expected out a couple weeks. Miami beat Pittsburgh 2-0 Tuesday behind Eury Perez (7 IP, 3 H, 7 K) and an Esteury Ruiz homer, its third straight win and 12th shutout of the season, improving to 61-58. Hosts Pittsburgh again tonight, Janson Junk starting.

Miami beat Pittsburgh 8-2 Wednesday on home runs from Griffin Conine and Heriberto Hernandez and six solid innings from Janson Junk - its fourth straight win, improving to 62-58. The NL wild-card picture: Cubs hold the top spot at 70-50, with Arizona and San Diego (both 64-57) holding the other two spots - Miami sits roughly 2.5-4.5 games back. Miami hosts Pittsburgh again today at 1:10pm.

Pittsburgh's Braxton Ashcraft threw a complete-game three-hitter (first Pirate to finish under 100 pitches since 2017) and rookie Rafael Flores hit two three-run homers for six RBIs as the Pirates routed Miami 13-1 Thursday, snapping the Marlins' win streak at four. Miami falls to 62-59. Updated wild-card picture: Cubs 71-50, Padres 65-57, Diamondbacks 64-58 - Miami trails the final spot by roughly 1.5 games. Opens a series at Cincinnati today.

Cincinnati's Chase Burns struck out eight over seven scoreless innings and outdueled Sandy Alcantara (7 IP, 1 ER on 3 H, 4 BB); Eugenio Suarez's sixth-inning RBI double was the game's only run in a 1-0 Reds win Friday - Miami's second straight loss. Marlins fall to 62-60. NL wild-card picture reshuffles: Cubs (71-51), Padres (65-57), and Phillies (65-58) now hold the three spots, Arizona just half a game back of the cutline - Miami trails the final spot by roughly 2.5 games. Series finale at Cincinnati tonight, 6:40pm ET.

Miami answered Friday's shutout with an 8-4 comeback win Saturday, scoring four runs in the eighth - Heriberto Hernandez's go-ahead two-run single, solo home runs from Jakob Marsee and Joe Mack - to even the Reds series at a game apiece and move to 63-60.

Miami beat Cincinnati 7-1 Sunday to take the series - Heriberto Hernandez's team-leading 18th home run and a Javier Sanoja three-run shot did the damage, with Eury Perez pitching well. Miami improves to 64-60, its second straight win.

Miami opens a series tonight at Philadelphia (67-58), which holds a wild-card spot alongside the Cubs and Padres; Miami trails by roughly three games with about six weeks left. Phillies starter Cristopher Sanchez owns a career 3-0 record and 1.06 ERA against Miami.

Philadelphia beat Miami 6-5 Monday night in a rain-affected series opener at Citizens Bank Park - Cristopher Sanchez picked up his MLB-leading 16th win, Jhoan Duran closed it out; Griffin Conine and Otto Lopez each drove in a run for Miami, and manager Clayton McCullough was ejected after a bases-loaded call was overturned. Miami falls to 64-61. The Phillies (68-58) hold a wild-card spot alongside the Cubs (73-53) and Padres (67-59); Miami's deficit widens with roughly six weeks left.

Philadelphia beat Miami 6-4 Tuesday - Bryson Stott's two-run single capped a four-run sixth off reliever Michael Petersen, and Cristopher Sanchez got his MLB-leading 16th win despite exiting after the sixth. It's Philadelphia's fifth straight win. Miami falls to 64-62, three games back of the final NL wild-card spot (Padres); the Phillies move a full game ahead of the Padres and two ahead of the Diamondbacks for the second wild-card spot outright.

Philadelphia beat Miami 4-1 Wednesday - Aaron Nola threw seven strong innings, Luis Arraez homered, Trea Turner added an RBI double off Sandy Alcantara - completing a three-game sweep and Philadelphia's sixth straight win, its best streak of the season, pulling the Phillies within 4.5 games of first-place Atlanta in the NL East. Miami falls to 64-63.

Miami was off Thursday after Wednesday's sweep; opens a three-game home series against Washington tonight (7:10pm, Ryan Gusto starting). NL wild-card picture has tightened into a scrum: San Diego and Philadelphia hold the two spots, Arizona sits roughly a game back of the cutline, and Miami (64-63) is bunched with the Cardinals, Reds, and Pirates about three games out. RHP Ronny Henriquez (60-day IL, UCL reconstruction) projected back the week of Aug. 24.

Miami beat Washington 3-2 in a Friday-night walk-off: Agustin Ramirez led off the 9th with a walk, a throwing error on an Esteury Ruiz infield hit put runners on 2nd and 3rd, Jakob Marsee was intentionally walked, and Javier Sanoja singled home the winner — Miami's sixth straight win over the Nationals. The Marlins improve to 65-64, back over .500. Chicago, Philadelphia, and San Diego now hold the three NL wild-card spots, with Arizona about a game back of the cutline and Miami bunched with St. Louis, Cincinnati, and Pittsburgh further behind. Miami hosts Washington again today at 4:10pm (Eury Perez vs. Jake Irvin), with Sunday's finale set (Janson Junk vs. Jackson Kent).

Miami beat Washington 4-2 Saturday on solo home runs from Heriberto Hernandez and Jakob Marsee, with Eury Perez working five innings — the Marlins' seventh straight win over the Nationals, improving to 66-64. Sunday's finale (Janson Junk vs. Jackson Kent) closes the series this afternoon.

Miami completed the sweep of Washington Sunday, 6-2, on Xavier Edwards' go-ahead two-run single, improving to 67-64 — eight straight wins over the Nationals. But the sweep didn't close the gap much: models now give Miami roughly 7.6% playoff odds, about four games behind San Diego for the final NL wild-card spot, with Chicago, Philadelphia, and San Diego holding the three spots and Arizona a game back of the cutline.

Boston beat Miami 4-2 Monday night at loanDepot Park -- Xavier Edwards' bases-loaded single put the Marlins ahead 2-1 in the seventh, but Anthony Seigler's go-ahead triple won it for the Red Sox. Miami's win streak, built entirely against last-place Washington, ended in its first game against a different opponent; Miami falls to 67-65.

Boston beat Miami again Tuesday night, 7-3, at loanDepot Park -- Miami's second straight loss to the Red Sox. What looked Monday like a single bad night now reads as a two-game skid immediately following the Washington sweep. Miami falls to 67-66.

Miami shut out Boston 4-0, avoiding a three-game sweep -- Ryan Gusto held the Red Sox to four hits over 5 2/3 innings, and Boston committed four errors. Miami improves to 68-66. NL wild-card picture: Cubs (76-57), Phillies (73-60), and Padres (71-62) hold the three spots, with Arizona 1.0 game back of the cutline.

Miami was idle Thursday while the three wild-card teams above them all won -- the gap widens to roughly four games back (Cubs 76-58, Phillies 74-60, Padres 72-62, Miami 68-66). The Marlins open a four-game series at Washington tonight at 6:45pm ET, Eury Perez (7-9, 3.17) against Brad Lord (5-2, 4.04); Miami is 8-1 against the Nationals this season and can lean on closer Pete Fairbanks (18 saves) in a close game.

Washington beat Miami 9-2 in Friday's series opener at Nationals Park -- a team the Marlins had beaten eight of nine times this season -- dropping Miami to 68-67 as the wild-card gap holds near four games with three games left in the series.

Washington completes the sweep: Miami lost 5-4 in 10 innings Saturday (Dylan Crews' walk-off RBI single) and 3-2 Sunday, falling to 68-69. The Cubs (76-59), Phillies (75-60), and Padres (72-63) hold the three NL wild-card spots -- Miami now sits roughly five games back with about a month left in the season.

Monday morning's fuller standings picture corrects the frame: the real cutline for the final NL wild-card spot is Arizona (73-65) and San Diego (72-65, half a game back), not the Cubs and Phillies, who are comfortably ahead for the other two spots. At 68-69, Miami sits roughly four and a half games back of Arizona with about a month left; the four-game series against Washington closes tonight before a three-game trip to Kansas City.

Washington closed out the series 6-3 as Daylen Lile hit two home runs -- his fourth multi-homer game of the year, 20th and 21st of the season -- taking 3 of 4 from Miami. The Marlins fall to 69-69. The wild-card picture flipped the same day: San Diego beat Cincinnati 5-0 to reach 73-65 while Arizona lost to Philadelphia 2-1 to fall to 73-66, handing the Padres a half-game lead over the Diamondbacks for the final NL wild-card spot -- the reverse of Sunday's order.

Miami beat Kansas City 6-3: Graham Pauley, recalled for his fifth call-up of the season, drove in a career-high four runs (a two-run homer and a two-run triple), Kyle Stowers added a 412-foot solo shot, and Tyler Phillips threw five innings of one-hit ball. Miami improves to 70-69. Both teams ahead of them for the final NL wild-card spot lost the same night -- San Diego fell to Cincinnati 4-3 (73-66) and Arizona fell to Philadelphia 7-1 (73-67) -- cutting Miami's deficit to three games with roughly three weeks left.

Miami beat Kansas City again Wednesday, 7-6, scoring three in the seventh to hold off a Royals team that had jumped out 5-1 in the first; the Marlins improve to 71-69. San Diego lost to Cincinnati 7-3, falling to 73-67, while Arizona beat Philadelphia 1-0 on a James McCann eighth-inning homer to improve to 74-67. Miami's wild-card deficit narrows to two games behind San Diego (2.5 behind Arizona) with the season's final three weeks underway.

Miami's two-game winning streak snapped: lost 7-3 to Kansas City, falling to 71-70. San Diego and Arizona's Thursday results were not confirmed at publication; last confirmed marks had them at 73-67 and 74-67 respectively.

Miami lost 6-1 to the Cubs at loanDepot Park Friday, falling to 71-71. The two teams play again Saturday afternoon. Confirmed weekend results for San Diego and Arizona were not available at publication time.

The Cubs beat Miami 6-5 Saturday, Miami's third straight loss, falling to 71-72. The deficit for the final NL wild-card spot is now four games behind Arizona, which reclaimed it the same night when San Diego lost to the Yankees, with 19 games left; CBS Sports' model had Miami at 1.3%.

Miami snapped its three-game skid with a 10-3 rout of the Cubs, Javier Sanoja and Heriberto Hernandez both homering, improving to 72-72. Arizona (75-68) and San Diego (75-68) both won too, holding the wild-card deficit at roughly three and a half games with 18 to play. Miami opens a series against the Mets Monday at loanDepot Park.

The Mets beat Miami 9-4 Monday night -- A.J. Ewing drove in three, Bo Bichette's go-ahead single broke a 4-4 tie in the fourth -- dropping the Marlins to 72-73. Arizona (76-68) holds the final NL wild-card spot with San Diego (75-68) half a game back; Miami's deficit widens to roughly four and a half games with 17 left to play. The two teams play again tonight, September 8, at 6:40pm ET at loanDepot Park.

The Mets beat Miami 7-5 Tuesday night -- Francisco Lindor led off the game with a home run and Juan Soto added a three-run shot as New York jumped ahead early and held on despite a shaky Sean Manaea outing. Miami falls to 72-74 and New York has already clinched the series. Arizona improved to 77-68 (an 11-inning win at Kansas City) and San Diego to 76-68 (a comeback win over Washington), still half a game apart for the final NL wild-card spot -- Miami's deficit widens to roughly five games with 16 left to play. The series finale is tonight, September 9, at 6:40pm ET at loanDepot Park.

The Mets completed a three-game sweep with a 15-14 win Wednesday -- New York led 8-0 in the third, Miami clawed back to lead 8-5 by the sixth, but the Mets scored six in the seventh (Lindor homered, Morel added an RBI single) and held on despite being outhit 20-15. Miami falls to 72-75, three games under .500 for the first time since June 9, roughly 6.5 games back of the final NL wild-card spot with 15 left; FanGraphs puts playoff odds at effectively zero.
Miami lost 6-2 to the Dodgers Friday at loanDepot Park, falling to 12th in the NL wild-card race with three games left -- effectively, if not yet mathematically, finished for the season.

Miami beat the Dodgers 4-3 Saturday, scoring three runs in the second inning and snapping Los Angeles's eight-game winning streak. The win is close to academic: Miami sits well outside the final NL wild-card spot, which San Diego holds by half a game over Arizona, with Miami, St. Louis, Pittsburgh, and Cincinnati all bunched roughly eight games back. The season closes today with the series finale at loanDepot Park.
Season finale: Miami beat the Dodgers 6-4 Sunday to close the regular season, finishing outside the NL wild-card picture. Thread resolved.

threads.title: Heat: the Giannis era begins
threads.current_state: Resolved: LeBron James signed with the Philadelphia 76ers, not Miami. The Heat's post-Giannis roster is now settled without further additions; Pat Riley said the team was disappointed but moves forward as built.

timeline.summary: Blockbuster trade lands the two-time MVP.
Roster construction and cap details public; Panthers release 2026-27 schedule.
Tim Hardaway Jr. signs one-year, $6.5M deal, filling out the wing rotation.
Heat's social team accidentally posts and deletes a LeBron introductory press conference link; ESPN reports Miami is one of three teams LeBron is weighing.
Heat confirm the page was real prep work published by mistake; Kalshi odds move to 51% from 39%; Rich Paul says no timetable exists.
LeBron James signs a two-year, $8M deal with the Philadelphia 76ers, not Miami; Rich Paul says James chose to preserve the memory of a title already won rather than risk a lesser second chapter.

threads.title: Dolphins rebuild under Hafley
threads.current_state: Miami opened its season with a 27-13 loss at Las Vegas (Willis passing for 220 yards with an interception and a rushing touchdown, sacked five times). Miami now travels to face San Francisco Sunday (4:25pm ET, Fox) as a roughly 13 to 13.5-point underdog; rookie S Kyle Louis is out (MCL), and Willis has a toe injury but is expected to play.

timeline.summary: Camp schedule announced.
Rookies reported; camp officially underway.
Jordyn Brooks signs three-year, $51.3M extension through 2029.
Joint-practice schedule confirmed: Aug. 12 at Washington, Aug. 20 hosting the Giants.
Veterans confirmed to report Tuesday, July 28; camp runs through Aug. 26 with the first public practice Aug. 2.
Veterans report as scheduled; training camp officially opens with the full squad on the field for the first time under Hafley.

First full practice: all veterans pass conditioning test; Achane fully participates after offseason shoulder surgery; Willie Gay Jr. sets an energetic tone; Chris Bell remains on PUP with no timetable.

Fuller Day One reporting: Willie Gay Jr.'s standout play was a one-handed interception returned for a touchdown off Cam Miller; Austin Jackson says he feels 'better than my normal self' after last year's rushed return from a toe injury.
Rookie safety Michael Taaffe intercepts backup quarterback Quinn Ewers, his former Texas teammate, in team drills.
Edge rusher Chop Robinson reports to camp carrying roughly ten added pounds of muscle.
Practice two runs as flagged - the hardest and longest of the week - with a shift toward individual and 11-on-11 work over 7-on-7 drills and an explicit emphasis on cutting penalties this season.

First public practice of camp runs as part of the NFL's 'Back Together Weekend,' free and open to fans, showcasing Malik Willis and rookies Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, and Chris Bell.
First practice in full pads this camp, testing Hafley's shift toward a power-based run scheme; Monday's session included a deep completion from Malik Willis to Tutu Atwell.
Practice 5, the second day in pads, tilts toward the defense with forced turnovers and the first one-on-one line periods of camp; Malik Willis connects with Malik Washington on two deep balls.

Thursday's practice: the defense forces four turnovers, including interceptions from Zayne Anderson and Ronnie Harrison Jr.; Hafley says Malik Willis's reps have grown more confident through the week, calling that the top thing he's watching for. Rookie WR Chris Bell continues rehab work on the side after a torn ACL.

Rookie DT Rene Konga is ruled out for the season; Miami signs DL Fatorma Mulbah to cover the spot and claims TE Jeremiah Franklin off waivers from New England, giving the roster six tight ends. Presumptive starting TE Greg Dulcich practices in a red non-contact jersey with an undisclosed injury, targeting a return around the Aug. 14 joint practice with Washington.

Friday's practice: CB Miles Battle had two interceptions (one a 50-plus-yard return), S Major Burns picked off a tipped pass, LB Jackson Woodard returned one for a touchdown, and DL Zach Sieler and edge Josh Uche each recorded sacks. Miami also signed S Tanner Wall, claimed CB Ahmari Harvey off waivers from Pittsburgh, and waived QB Mark Gronowski and S Omar Brown (injured).

Saturday's fan-open scrimmage at Hard Rock Stadium: seven players out injured (Ferrell, Brents, Trader Jr., L. Johnson Jr., Sims, Coleman Jr., Salyer); Dulcich progressed in a red non-contact jersey. Offensive highlights: deep completions from Willis to Traore, Miller to Washington, and Ewers to Marshall.

Miami practices at Hard Rock Stadium for the first time this camp; QB Malik Willis has a strong day, including two 20-plus-yard completions on scrambles to Tutu Atwell and Seydou Traore. Team is off in the afternoon.

Monday opens with a free public practice, 9:30am. Wednesday's joint practice with Washington is confirmed for Ashburn, VA - the Commanders' first hosted joint-practice partner since 2018 - ahead of Friday's 7pm preseason opener at Northwest Stadium. The Saturday injury list has no confirmed resolution yet.
Miami travels to Ashburn, VA ahead of tomorrow's joint practice with Washington. The injury list and Dulcich's status remain unresolved heading into it.

Miami runs today's joint practice at Washington's Ashburn, VA facility - the first-ever joint practice held on Commanders Park grounds. Dulcich still in a red non-contact jersey but trending toward a return. Injury-list detail sharpens: Ferrell out multiple weeks, Brents out this week, Coleman Jr./Trader Jr./Sims probably out this week with a possible return next week; kicker Zane Gonzalez newly out for weeks.

Wednesday's joint practice at Washington's Ashburn facility gave Miami its first outside benchmark of camp, and the Commanders' defensive front won it - Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson repeatedly beat Miami's offensive line for would-be sacks, and Mike Sainristil returned an interception for a touchdown. Miami's own defense and injury list were not the story of the day. Team preps for tomorrow's 7pm preseason opener against Washington at Northwest Stadium.

Miami plays its preseason opener at Washington tonight, 7pm at Northwest Stadium - Hafley's first game as head coach and Malik Willis's Miami debut. Miami is a 3-point favorite, but most starters are expected to rest after the extensive joint-practice work; rookie CB Chris Johnson intercepted Quinn Ewers in Wednesday's team drills, and OT Austin Jackson is fully cleared from his toe injury.

Washington won Jeff Hafley's debut as Miami's head coach 20-7 Friday night at Northwest Stadium. Miami's starters opened with a 14-play, 93-yard touchdown drive capped by a De'Von Achane score, but Washington's defense took over after that, forcing a turnover on downs and back-to-back three-and-outs, with most Miami starters resting for the rest of the game.
